To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a common haplotyope, including the α5 nicotinic receptor gene, is associated with increased risk for NA among individuals with European origin.

a common mis-sense variant of the CHRNA5 subunit of the α4β2 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor increases the risk of NA, that this risk is mediated in part by decreased calcium permeability of the receptor and more rapid receptor desensitization and that the CHRNA5–CHRNA3–CHRNA4 gene cluster is the first common genetic risk factor for NA to be identified.
a mis-sense variant in CHRNA5 is the strongest genetic risk factor identified for NA to date.

the genetic architecture of NA and the biology of the nicotinic receptors, which may provide a basis for novel pharmacotherapy.
identifying the genetic influences on NA, which may help us understand its biology, which may in turn help us develop more effective treatments.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a single gene, or a single genetic mechanism, is not the cause of NA, but that there is a genetic influence on NA that has been identified in a region of chromosome 15.

there is a common risk allele in the CHRNA3–A3–CHRNA5 region that increases risk for NA, but that there are also other genetic influences on the risk of NA in this region that have not been fully identified.
a genetic variant in the CHRNA3–5–A4 region increases risk for NA, but the effect size is small and the biological mechanism(s) are not well understood.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the CHRNA5–CHRNA3–CHRNA4 region of the genome confers risk for NA, and that the risk allele at the CHRNA5 locus (D398N) is a functional polymorphism, which is a reasonable candidate for therapeutic intervention.
a genetic variant in the CHRNA4–5–3 gene cluster is implicated in NA, but that this is only one of many genetic influences on NA.
the CHRNA5–CHRNA3–CHRNB4 region has been implicated in NA and that the 398N allele of the mis-sense single nucleotide polymorphism is a risk allele.

there is a genetic risk region for NA that is shared across different populations, but the specific genetic variants and biological mechanisms that underlie this risk region are still unknown.
